clinicalPearls: Defined by the triad of liver disease or portal hypertension, arterial hypoxaemia, and intrapulmonary vascular dilatations causing abnormal gas exchange
Characterised physiologically by intrapulmonary vasodilatation and shunting rather than by raised pulmonary pressures, distinguishing it from portopulmonary hypertension
Classically produces platypnoea and orthodeoxia, with breathlessness and desaturation that worsen on sitting or standing and improve on lying flat

Contrast (bubble) echocardiography is the key diagnostic test, showing delayed appearance of microbubbles in the left heart after several cardiac cycles, indicating an intrapulmonary rather than intracardiac shunt
Arterial blood gases reveal hypoxaemia with a widened alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient
Spider naevi and clubbing may accompany the underlying liver disease and correlate with more severe vasodilatation
Liver transplantation is the only definitive treatment and can reverse the hypoxaemia; supplemental oxygen is supportive in the interim
reference.pathophysiology: Hepatopulmonary syndrome results from abnormal dilatation of the pulmonary microvasculature in the presence of liver disease or portal hypertension. Impaired hepatic clearance and portosystemic shunting lead to excess circulating vasodilators, particularly increased nitric oxide production within the pulmonary vasculature, which dilates the precapillary and capillary bed. These dilated vessels allow mixed venous blood to pass too rapidly and across too wide a channel for oxygen to diffuse to the centre of the enlarged capillary, producing a diffusion-perfusion defect, and true anatomical shunts may also form. Because the dilated vessels predominate at the lung bases, upright posture increases basal perfusion and worsens shunting, generating the characteristic orthodeoxia and platypnoea. The result is arterial hypoxaemia with a widened alveolar-arterial gradient in the absence of raised pulmonary artery pressures.
additionalDifferentials: Intracardiac right-to-left shunt (e.g. patent foramen ovale)
Pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (e.g. hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast (agitated saline bubble) echocardiography to demonstrate delayed intrapulmonary shunting
Arterial blood gas analysis, ideally supine and upright, to document hypoxaemia and orthodeoxia
Measurement of the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient
Technetium-labelled macroaggregated albumin lung perfusion scan to quantify shunt fraction
Chest imaging and pulmonary function tests to exclude parenchymal or airway disease
Assessment of liver disease severity and portal hypertension
redFlags: Severe resting hypoxaemia requiring high supplemental oxygen
Marked orthodeoxia limiting the patient to a recumbent posture
Progressive desaturation indicating advancing intrapulmonary shunting
Coexisting features suggesting portopulmonary hypertension, which alters transplant risk
reference.prognosis: Hepatopulmonary syndrome worsens the prognosis of underlying liver disease and progressive hypoxaemia can be disabling, but liver transplantation reverses the intrapulmonary vasodilatation in most patients, often with gradual resolution of hypoxaemia over months. Severe hypoxaemia raises transplant risk yet also strengthens the indication, as no effective medical therapy exists.
pitfalls: Mistaking hepatopulmonary syndrome for portopulmonary hypertension despite their opposite pulmonary vascular physiology
Attributing hypoxaemia to coexisting lung disease and not performing contrast echocardiography
Overlooking orthodeoxia by measuring oxygenation only in the supine position
Failing to consider the syndrome in a breathless cirrhotic patient with clubbing and spider naevi
Assuming supplemental oxygen is definitive treatment rather than a supportive bridge to transplantation
references: ESC/ERS Guidelines for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Pulmonary Hypertension
Sherlock's Diseases of the Liver and Biliary System
management: Liver transplantation is the only definitive therapy, reversing intrapulmonary vascular dilatation and hypoxaemia over months; refer suitable candidates to a transplant centre early
Long-term supplemental oxygen to correct hypoxaemia and relieve breathlessness, including ambulatory oxygen for exertional and postural desaturation
Optimise management of the underlying liver disease and portal hypertension
Consider transcatheter embolisation of discrete large intrapulmonary arteriovenous communications in selected patients with refractory hypoxaemia
Serial monitoring with arterial blood gases and pulse oximetry, measured supine and upright, to track orthodeoxia and progression, and to support transplant prioritisation as severity increases
Multidisciplinary hepatology, respiratory and transplant input for coordinated assessment and listing
